questions.enonce_markdown:
Which points on the figure above show the use of:

(i) efficient methods of production? (3 marks)

(ii) inefficient methods of production? (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Reading the figure.** The curve BGH is the production possibility curve (PPC, also called the production possibility frontier). It shows the maximum combinations of tractors and banana that the economy can produce when all its resources are fully employed and used with the best known technology.

**(i) Efficient methods of production: points B, G and H.**

- B (0 tons of banana, 30 tractors), G (20 tons of banana, 25 tractors) and H (35 tons of banana, 0 tractors) all lie **on** the curve.
- At each of them the economy uses all its resources fully and efficiently: more of one good can be obtained only by giving up some of the other. This is productive efficiency.

**(ii) Inefficient methods of production: points A and F.**

- A (5 tons, 5 tractors) and F (25 tons, 15 tractors) lie **inside** the curve.
- The economy can produce these combinations, but it is wasting resources: some factors are unemployed or underemployed, or they are badly organised. Output could be increased, without sacrificing the other good, by moving to the curve.

**Note.** Point Z lies **outside** the curve: it is unattainable with the present resources and technology (see part (d)).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Suppose a country is at point **B** on the figure above and wants to move to point **G**;

(i) What will be the opportunity cost of producing banana? (2 marks)

(ii) What type of opportunity cost is shown by the figure above? (1 mark)

(iii) Identify the shapes associated with the other two types of opportunity cost. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Opportunity cost of producing banana (B to G).**

- At B the country produces 30 tractors and no banana. At G it produces 25 tractors and 20 tons of banana.
- To gain 20 tons of banana it gives up $30 - 25 = 5$ tractors.
- **Opportunity cost of 20 tons of banana = 5 tractors**, that is $\dfrac{5}{20} = 0.25$ tractor for each additional ton of banana (equivalently, one tractor is given up for every 4 tons of banana).

**(ii) Type of opportunity cost: increasing (rising) opportunity cost.**

- The PPC is bowed outwards (concave to the origin), so its slope becomes steeper as more banana is produced.
- Check with the figure: from B to G each ton of banana costs 0.25 tractor, but from G to H (banana rises from 20 to 35 tons, tractors fall from 25 to 0) each ton costs $\dfrac{25}{15} \approx 1.67$ tractors. The cost of banana rises as more of it is produced.
- Reason: resources are not equally suited to both goods. The first resources moved to banana are those best suited to it (cheap to move); later the economy has to move resources that are better at making tractors, so more tractors are lost for each extra ton of banana.

**(iii) Shapes associated with the other two types of opportunity cost.**

- **Constant opportunity cost:** a **straight line** PPC sloping downwards (constant slope). Each unit of one good always costs the same number of units of the other, because the resources are equally suited (perfectly substitutable) to both uses.
- **Decreasing opportunity cost:** a PPC that is **bowed inwards (convex to the origin)**. The slope becomes flatter as more of the good on the horizontal axis is produced, because of economies of scale and gains from specialisation: each extra unit costs fewer units of the other good.

questions.enonce_markdown: State four assumptions of the Production Possibility Curve. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A PPC is drawn under the following assumptions (any four, one mark each):

1. **Only two goods** are produced (here tractors and banana), so that the trade-off can be shown on a two-dimensional diagram.
2. **Resources are fixed** in quantity and quality (the supplies of land, labour, capital and enterprise do not change) over the period considered.
3. **Full employment of resources:** all available factors of production are employed.
4. **Productive efficiency:** the resources are used in the best possible way, so that the frontier shows the maximum output.
5. **The state of technology is given** (constant) for the period.
6. **Resources can be moved between the two uses**, but they are not equally suited to both (this explains the bowed shape when opportunity cost increases).
7. The analysis is for a **given period of time** (a static picture).

questions.enonce_markdown: List four conditions for a country to produce at point **Z** on the figure above.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Reading the figure.** Point Z lies outside the present frontier BGH, so it cannot be reached with the existing resources and technology. A country can produce at Z only if the PPC **shifts outwards** (economic growth) so that Z lies on or inside the new curve, and if the country then uses its resources efficiently. Four conditions (any four):

1. **An increase in the quantity of factors of production:** discovery or exploitation of new natural resources (for example oil, minerals, new farmland), growth of the labour force, or capital accumulation through investment in machines, factories and roads.
2. **An improvement in the quality of the factors:** better education, training and health care (human capital), giving a more productive labour force.
3. **Technological progress and innovation:** better machines, seeds, methods and management, so that more tractors and more banana can be produced from the same resources.
4. **Better organisation and efficiency, and a favourable environment:** better infrastructure (transport, electricity), political stability and sound institutions, and efficient use of all the resources so that the economy is on, not inside, the new curve.
5. **Access to external resources:** foreign investment, aid, technology transfer and international trade, which allow the country to consume beyond what it could produce alone.

**Conclusion.** Z is reached only by long-run growth (an outward shift of the PPC) combined with full and efficient use of resources.
